import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Green's Open Problem 9

References:
- [Gr24] [Green, Ben. "100 open problems." (2024).](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/greenbj/papers/open-problems.pdf#problem.9)
- [BlSi20] Bloom, Thomas F., and Olof Sisask. "Breaking the logarithmic barrier in Roth's theorem on
  arithmetic progressions." arXiv preprint arXiv:2007.03528 (2020).
-/

open Filter

namespace Green9

/--
The quantity $r_k(N)$, defined as the size of the largest subset of $\{1, \dots, N\}$ without
non-trivial $k$-term arithmetic progressions.
-/
noncomputable def r (k N : ℕ) : ℕ := (Finset.Icc 1 N).maxAPFreeCard k

/--
Problem 9 (i): is $r_3(N) \ll N(\log N)^{-10}$?

Solved in [BlSi20].
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5]
theorem green_9_i :
    (fun (N : ℕ) ↦ (r 3 N : ℝ)) ≪ fun (N : ℕ) ↦ (N : ℝ) * (Real.log N) ^ (-10 : ℝ) := by
  sorry

/--
Problem 9 (ii): is $r_5(N) \ll N(\log N)^{-c}$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5]
theorem green_9_ii : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∃ c > (0 : ℝ), (fun (N : ℕ) ↦ (r 5 N : ℝ))
      ≪ fun (N : ℕ) ↦ (N : ℝ) * (Real.log N) ^ (-c) := by
  sorry

/--
Problem 9 (iii): is $r_4(\mathbf{F}_5^n) \ll N^{1-c}$, where $N=5^n$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5]
theorem green_9_iii : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∃ c > (0 : ℝ), (fun (n : ℕ) ↦ ((Finset.univ : Finset (𝔽₅ n)).maxAPFreeCard 4 : ℝ))
      ≪ fun (n : ℕ) ↦ ((5 : ℝ) ^ n) ^ (1 - c) := by
  sorry

-- TODO(jeangud): Add some additional bounds from the literature.

end Green9

findings.description: The docstring's attribution “Solved in [BlSi20]” cites the wrong paper. The referenced 2020 paper proves r₃(N) ≪ N/(log N)^(1+c) for a very small positive c, not the exponent-10 bound in this declaration. The Lean statement itself matches Green's problem, and its `research solved` category is correct.
findings.source_evidence: Green, “100 open problems,” Problem 9(i) and its 2024 update (pp. 6–7), attributes the breakthrough to Kelley–Meka and cites Bloom–Sisask's 2023 improvement as reference [39]: https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/greenbj/papers/open-problems.pdf#problem.9. In arXiv:2007.03528, Theorem 1.1 gives N/(log N)^(1+c), and the following paragraph explicitly says any c produced by that method would be very small. By contrast, Theorem 1 of arXiv:2309.02353 gives N exp(−c(log N)^(1/9)), which implies the exponent-10 bound.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the attribution and bibliography entry with Bloom and Sisask, “An improvement to the Kelley-Meka bounds on three-term arithmetic progressions,” arXiv:2309.02353 (2023), or cite Kelley–Meka's original breakthrough. Leave the Lean statement and category unchanged.

reformulations.difference: The shared AP predicate expresses non-triviality through exact set cardinality rather than an explicit positive common difference.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For k ≥ 2 in ℕ, a nonzero difference is positive and makes the k terms a+i*d distinct. A zero difference produces at most one distinct element and cannot satisfy the cardinality requirement. Thus the AP-free predicates, and consequently their maximum subset sizes, agree. A progression with negative integer difference can be reversed. The relevant natural-number predicate equivalence and equality with a bounded, computable maximum were proved in /workspace/review/ap-equivalence.lean.

reformulations.difference: The expanded definition of r₄(𝔽₅ⁿ) excludes set-valued progressions with exactly four distinct elements, rather than explicitly excluding progressions with nonzero vector difference.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Every nonzero vector in 𝔽₅ⁿ has additive order 5, so its first four progression terms are distinct. Conversely, four distinct terms rule out a zero difference. This equivalence holds also for n = 0, when neither kind of non-trivial progression exists. The predicate equivalence and equality of the resulting maxima were proved in /workspace/review/ap-equivalence.lean.

sources_consulted: Ben Green, “100 open problems”: https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/greenbj/papers/open-problems.pdf#problem.9 — notation on p. 2, Problem 9 and all its comments on pp. 6–7, and references [39] and [194].

Thomas F. Bloom and Olof Sisask, “Breaking the logarithmic barrier in Roth's theorem on arithmetic progressions,” arXiv:2007.03528 — LaTeX source from https://arxiv.org/e-print/2007.03528, especially the abstract, Theorem 1.1, the paragraph about its constant, and concluding remarks.

Thomas F. Bloom and Olof Sisask, “An improvement to the Kelley-Meka bounds on three-term arithmetic progressions,” arXiv:2309.02353 — LaTeX source from https://arxiv.org/e-print/2309.02353, especially the abstract, introductory discussion, Theorem 1, and bibliography.

review.notes: All four declarations were checked. No mathematical misformalizations were found, and Green's source agrees with the solved/open/open categories. Successful Lean experiments are in /workspace/review/boundaries.lean, ap-equivalence.lean, and asymptotics.lean. They check empty and small inputs, prove the relevant AP-definition equivalences, and show that the atTop bounds are equivalent to uniform bounds for N ≥ 2 in parts (i)–(ii), and for all n in part (iii). Thus log(0), log(1), and dimension zero cause no defect. Computable versions proved equal to the definitions were tested through N = 10 for r₃ and r₅, and in dimensions 0 and 1 for the finite-field maximum. The equivalence proofs do not depend on sorryAx.
